A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DOMINO benchmark and PUMA model. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching the retained embedded animation frames across versions.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation experiments, including baseline comparisons, PUMA ablations, and static/dynamic transfer evaluations in Section 4 and Appendix D.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original real-robot results, inference measurements, and further ablation and generalization experiments.

M1.justification: PUMA retains its historical optical flow, action/world queries, object-centric future supervision, action loss, and auxiliary cosine loss. The three-stage data-collection description makes the previously described dynamic execution stage explicit. Additional implementation disclosures and LoRA transfer experiments do not establish a redesign of the core method.

E1.justification: v3 extends the simulation evaluation to five physical AgileX Piper manipulation tasks, including Lift Bottle as an adaptation of Shake Bottle. It also evaluates unseen speed conditions: alpha=0.05 and randomized alpha in [0.5, 1.5]. These substantially expand deployment-domain and environmental coverage beyond v1.

E2.justification: ContextVLA, previously only cited, is newly evaluated against PUMA on the 10-task subset in v3 Table 10. The comparator membership of the main Table 3 remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 introduces real-robot protocols with 50 demonstrations and 20 trials per task, 10-task transfer experiments comparing direct training with Level-1 initialization and LoRA, doubled-data experiments, and a controlled latency benchmark. The retained training description changes per-device batch size from 16 to 8; Table 3 also revises InternVLA-M1's stated backbone from InternVL to Qwen2.5-VL. These disclosures do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's retained component ablations and ACT complexity analysis, v3 adds task-type breakdowns, a history-aware comparator, history-length and N=6 prediction-horizon tests, cross-level transfer, speed-shift robustness, and doubled-data analysis. Appendix C also adds simulation and physical-policy rollout examples. These address substantially more questions about PUMA's behavior.

E5.justification: Section 4.6 newly specifies latency averaging over 500 inference queries after 50 warm-ups, adding repeated-measurement reporting absent from v1. Neither version reports multi-seed training variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. No increased repetition of the retained success-rate experiments is established.

E6.justification: The headline Table 3 result remains 17.20% SR and 34.97 MS. Substantial new results include physical-robot SR of 42% for PUMA versus 24% for pi0.5, and 10-task SR of 20.9% versus ContextVLA's 7.8%. The extended horizon ablation reports 13.62% at N=6 versus 17.20% at N=4, adding evidence that longer prediction is not uniformly beneficial.

T1.justification: Appendix D.3 adds explicit mathematical specifications for trajectory generation, including back-calculation equations, clipped half-normal speed sampling, and segment-mixture probabilities. The POMDP, metric definitions, and learning objectives remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof. The new speed distribution conflicts with the uniform specification retained in Section 2.3.

C1.justification: The principal claims remain the DOMINO dynamic-manipulation benchmark, PUMA's combination of historical motion and future prediction, its approximately 6.3-point success-rate advantage, and transfer benefits from dynamic data. The added experiments broaden support without redefining the abstract and introduction's central contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.4 replaces the assertion that dynamic manipulation subsumes static skills with a qualification about overlapping manipulation primitives. New discussions interpret history length, excessive prediction horizons, and cross-level transfer. Appendix F adds substantive failure modes and limitations concerning stop-on-contact dynamics, bimanual coordination, control delays, and sim-to-real errors.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies Qwen3-VL-4B initialization, hidden dimension, the 14-dimensional action head, absence of additional proprioceptive input, DINOv2-B/14 supervision, and distributed-training details. It also documents trajectory construction and rejection rules, physical motion generation using strings, and real-robot adaptation. A project-page link is added while the code URL is retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds references and brief positioning concerning autonomous-driving VLAs, parallel task execution, 3D understanding, and scene-level world models, plus an AdamW citation. The original related-work framework and central distinction from prior manipulation methods remain. Numerous venue updates refer to the same previously cited works.

P1.justification: Most original prose and section ordering are retained. v3 makes local wording and cross-reference corrections, shortens the conclusion, adds experimental subsections, and reorganizes the expanded appendix with author contributions and discussion sections. This is a limited editorial revision alongside substantial new scientific content.

P2.justification: v3 adds a physical-robot setup/results figure, simulation and real-world rollout panels, a data-generation schematic, and tables for task categories, transfer, latency, and extended analyses. Existing figures and result tables are largely retained and renumbered, while the new displays substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v1's PUMA evidence was concentrated in Level-1 simulation. v3 substantially strengthens validation through physical-robot experiments, cross-difficulty and speed-shift tests, and targeted history/prediction controls. Fuller implementation disclosures and explicit limitations also improve reproducibility and interpretation. The physical study remains small, uncertainty intervals are absent, and the sampling descriptions are inconsistent, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and transparency.
